title: AI and the trusted advisor: What should you expect from a services provider now?
summary: This blog explores four ways to assess trusted advisors in the age of AI, including how to evaluate their genuine experience, sound judgment and trusted advice.
body_markdown:
Nearly two years ago, I published a blog,[Will the real trusted advisor please stand up?](https://www.cgi.com/en/blog/managed-it-outsourcing-services/will-real-trusted-advisor-please-stand-up) I made the argument that trusted advisor status is not something a provider can just claim; it must be earned.


I offered three questions to help buyers of IT and business consulting services tell a genuine advisor from a capable solution specialist:


1. Do they understand your industry and your business?
2. What was the focus of your first meeting with them?
3. How do they engage?


In the age of advanced AI, those questions still work; however, AI has devalued several of the signals buyers used to rely on. Unfortunately, the signals you used to trust are now easy to manufacture.


## Recognizing genuine understanding in the age of AI


In the past, a provider who arrived informed about your industry, competitors, recent earnings updates and top challenges had taken the time to understand your business. That effort suggested interest, and interest suggested commitment. Today, that same briefing takes about 20 minutes to generate with a well-written prompt.


This is not an argument against AI. It is a useful tool, and providers who use it well can serve you better. But as AI makes it easier to gather and present information about your business, a provider’s apparent preparation tells you less about the depth of their understanding.


It is now more challenging to distinguish someone who truly understands your business from someone who can describe it convincingly. This means vendor evaluations and the process for qualifying potential trusted advisors needs to focus on qualities that AI alone cannot establish.


## A trusted advisor helps ask the right questions


Most executives I speak with are doing more research before they contact a provider. They can define a problem, explore the market, compare options and draft a business case without speaking to a vendor. This preparation gives them more context and leverage when they evaluate providers.


Yet this shift in behavior does create a risk. AI can quickly answer the questions being asked to solve a business problem; however, AI may not flag that the question rests on a mistaken assumption or a deeper issue. AI may also provide a proposed solution that has failed at similar organizations for reasons that were never made public.


By the time providers are invited in, executives may have settled on how to define the problem and moved straight to execution. If that initial definition is wrong, things can move in the wrong direction faster.


A trusted advisor should help you test your assumptions and make sure you are solving the right problem. That ability deserves close attention when evaluating providers.


## Four ways to assess a trusted advisor beyond AI


AI can help leaders research options, compare approaches and prepare for conversations with providers. Now the focus of those conversations can assess areas beyond what a provider knows, such as sound judgment, a willingness to question assumptions, and support in decision making.


### Follow these four checks to determine whether a provider can contribute as a trusted advisor.


> 1. **Evidence of experience.**
>
>
> Information may be easy to find; experience comes from doing the work. Ask what they would do differently if they ran a comparable program again. Listen for specific lessons: what went wrong, what impact it had and how they responded. Notice whether they share those insights openly or only after you ask.
> 2. **Willingness to challenge your assumptions.**
>
>
> In an early conversation, a provider should ask questions to confirm that you are addressing the right problem, at the right level, and whether your proposed approach is likely to work. If they agree with your view throughout, ask what risks or alternatives they see. Their answer can show whether they have considered the issue from different angles.
> 3. **Useful engagement from the start.** A strong provider offers useful expertise while you are still forming your view: relevant insights, access to specialists with experience in your industry, and opportunities to explore options at your own pace. Consider whether they are helpful before a buying decision is on the table.
> 4. **Support for the decision as well as the solution.** Major investments raise questions beyond technical design. A trusted advisor should help you work through questions such as: Why should we do this? Why now? What outcome do we seek? What needs to be true for it to work? What risks are we accepting, and how will we manage them? Notice whether the provider explores these questions with you so that you are prepared to make the final decision or recommendation with confidence.


## What makes a trusted advisor has not changed with AI


In my first blog, I described four pillars of a trusted advisor relationship: shared culture and values, mutual trust and respect, commitment to business outcomes, and a long-term vision. Those qualities remain essential. AI has changed how easily a provider can appear to demonstrate them, making it more important to look for evidence in how they work with you.


Access to information is no longer a differentiator on its own. The partners worth having help you turn information into insight, insight into candid dialogue, and dialogue into decisions you can confidently explain to your board.


The bar is higher than it was two years ago. You should expect providers to meet it.
